lessons.unit: Unit 1: Knowing Allah (Aqeedah)
lessons.title: Who is Allah? Tawhid, the Oneness of Allah
objectives: Explain that Tawhid means Allah is One
Recite and explain the meaning of Surah al-Ikhlas
Give examples of things that only Allah can do

keywords.def: believing that Allah is One, with no partner
Lord: the One who creates, owns, cares for and controls everything
the Eternal Refuge whom all creation needs while He needs none
worship: everything we do to please Allah alone

starter: Say the bismillah aloud. What does it mean in English?
Name three things Allah has created that you can see from your window.
What is the first pillar of Islam, and what words do we say for it?

teach.heading: Bismillah: starting with Allah
bullets: We begin in the name of Allah, the Most Kind, the Most Merciful
Allah is our Creator, our Lord (Rabb)
Today: what does it mean that Allah is One?
teach.note: Begin with bismillah together. Ask: why do Muslims start things with Allah’s name? Take 2-3 answers (to get blessing, to remember Him, to do good). Link to the kalimah they already know. Misconception to listen for: that Allah is ‘like’ something we can picture. Say gently that we do not imagine Allah’s form.

teach.heading: What does Tawhid mean?
bullets: Tawhid means believing Allah is One
He has no partner, no helper and no children
Only Allah creates, owns and controls everything
Only Allah deserves to be worshipped
teach.note: Write ‘ahad’ = one, unique. Give the example of a school: there is one headteacher in charge, but nobody is in charge of Allah. Careful: analogies are only for understanding, nothing is like Allah (Qur’an 42:11, say it in simple English: ‘There is nothing like Him’). Ask: what could someone worship wrongly (idols, money, fame)?

teach.heading: Surah al-Ikhlas (112)
bullets: “Say: He is Allah, the One.”
“Allah, the Eternal Refuge.”
“He neither begets nor is born.”
“And there is none equal to Him.”
teach.note: Recite the surah slowly in Arabic then read the meaning. Explain ‘as-Samad’: everyone needs Him, He needs no one. Ask: who do you need every day? (parents, food, water) Then: does Allah need any of these? Highlight: this short surah sums up Tawhid. Many reports tell us it is a great surah; just say we love to recite it in our prayers.

teach.heading: Only Allah
bullets: Allah gives life and takes it back
Allah provides rizq: food, water, health
Allah hears every du’a, near or far
So we ask Allah alone for help
teach.note: Link to Surah al-Fatihah: ‘You alone we worship, You alone we ask for help.’ Ask: when you are scared or ill, who do you call upon? Give the idea that we can ask people for help they are able to give (a teacher helps with homework) but we ask Allah for what only He can do (to guide hearts, to heal, to forgive).

teach.heading: Living with Tawhid
bullets: Pray to Allah only
Put trust in Allah after working hard
Be grateful: say alhamdulillah
Be honest, because Allah sees us
teach.note: Make it practical. ‘Tawakkul’ means trust: explain it as ‘do your best, then rely on Allah’. Take 2 volunteers to give a real-life example (before a test, when losing something).

practice: Complete the sentence: Tawhid means believing that ______.
Match the ayah to its meaning: ‘Allahus-Samad’ / ‘Lam yalid wa lam yulad’ / ‘Qul huwa Allahu ahad’.
Give two things that only Allah can do and two things people can do.
independent: Write four sentences explaining Tawhid to a younger child in Year 2.
Draw and label a poster for Surah al-Ikhlas with each ayah and its meaning.
List three ways we show we believe in Tawhid at home or school.
lessons.homework: Learn Surah al-Ikhlas by heart with its meaning and write one sentence about each ayah.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide the surah with transliteration and a picture clue for each ayah; stretch: explain why Tawhid is the most important belief in Islam.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Knowing Allah (Aqeedah)
lessons.title: The Beautiful Names of Allah
objectives: Know that Allah has beautiful names
Explain the meaning of at least six names
Say how a Muslim can reflect on these names in daily life

keywords.def: the most beautiful names of Allah
the Most Gracious, whose mercy covers everything
the Most Merciful, especially to the believers
the Creator

starter: What does Tawhid mean?
Recite Surah al-Ikhlas together and give its meaning.
Name one thing only Allah can do.

teach.heading: Allah has beautiful names
bullets: “To Allah belong the best names, so call upon Him by them” (7:180)
Each name tells us about Allah’s perfect qualities
We learn them from the Qur’an and authentic Sunnah
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Explain that we know Allah’s names only from what He and His Messenger ﷺ told us; we do not make up names. Ask: why do we learn names of people we love? Link to getting to know Allah better. Sound idea: we call on Allah by names that fit our du’a, for example ‘Ya Ghafur, forgive me’.

teach.heading: Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim
bullets: Ar-Rahman: Allah’s mercy reaches all creation
Ar-Rahim: His special mercy for believers
Both are in the bismillah and al-Fatihah
teach.note: Show the bismillah and point at the two names. Ask: what are signs of mercy you can see in the world (rain, sunlight, a mother’s love)? Point out that all mercy in the world comes from Allah. Misconception: that Allah’s mercy means there is no accountability. Say we hope for His mercy and still try our best.

teach.heading: Al-Khaliq, Ar-Razzaq, as-Sami’
bullets: Al-Khaliq: the Creator who made everything
Ar-Razzaq: the Provider of all provision
As-Sami’: the All-Hearing
Al-Basir: the All-Seeing
teach.note: Use real examples: how does a seed grow into fruit? Who provides? Then: Allah hears a whisper from under the blanket at night. Ask: how should knowing Allah sees us change our behaviour when no one is looking? Link to honesty in tests.

teach.heading: Al-Ghafur and At-Tawwab
bullets: Al-Ghafur: the Forgiving
At-Tawwab: the One who accepts repentance
We say astaghfirullah when we make mistakes
We forgive others too
teach.note: Explain tawbah simply: stop the wrong, feel sorry, promise not to return, and put it right with anyone harmed. Ask: when someone says sorry to you what should you do? Keep a calm, hopeful tone: Allah loves those who return to Him (Qur’an 2:222 says Allah loves those who repent; you may mention this in your own words).

teach.heading: Using the names in our lives
bullets: Remember Allah in good times and hard times
Call on Allah with a fitting name in du’a
Try to show mercy, honesty and kindness
teach.note: Model a du’a: ‘Ya Razzaq, provide for me what is good.’ Ask pupils to choose a name that suits a situation (feeling worried, wanting to be forgiven). Remind them that we reflect good character, we are never like Allah, but He loves mercy in people.

practice: Match each name with its meaning: Al-Khaliq, Ar-Razzaq, As-Sami’, Al-Ghafur.
Which name would you use in a du’a when you have made a mistake? Explain why.
Fill in the missing word: Ar-Rahman means the Most ______.
independent: Make a colourful mind map with six names of Allah, their meanings and one example of each in daily life.
Write a short du’a using at least two names of Allah.
Explain in three sentences why it helps a Muslim to know Allah’s names.
exit: Give the meaning of two names of Allah.
Why should we only use names of Allah that come from the Qur’an and Sunnah?
lessons.homework: Learn six names of Allah with their meanings and use one in a du’a this evening.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: name cards with picture clues and Arabic/English pairs; stretch: explain the difference between Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Knowing Allah (Aqeedah)
lessons.title: Signs of Allah in creation
objectives: Explain what an ayah (sign) of Allah is
Give examples of signs in the universe
Respond to creation with gratitude and care

keywords.def: a sign; also a verse of the Qur’an
everything Allah has made
gratitude to Allah
a trustee who looks after the earth

starter: Give the meaning of Ar-Razzaq and Al-Khaliq.
Say two names of Allah that show mercy.
What does ‘Subhanallah’ mean when we say it?

teach.heading: Signs for people who think
bullets: “In the creation of the heavens and the earth ... are signs for people of understanding” (3:190)
Allah invites us to look, think and wonder
Science and faith both begin with noticing
teach.note: Start with bismillah. Read Qur’an 3:190 in English slowly. Ask pupils what they notice in nature on the way to school or from their window. Point out that Islam encourages reflection. Avoid presenting faith and science as enemies; observing the world is a way to see Allah’s signs.

teach.heading: Signs in the sky and the earth
bullets: The sun gives light and warmth at the right distance
Night and day follow one another
Rain brings dead land back to life
Mountains, seas and animals show Allah’s wisdom
teach.note: Bring in age-appropriate facts: the water cycle, the rotation of the earth for day and night. Ask: what would happen if the sun were much closer? Draw out the idea of balance and order. Remember: we say the universe points to a Creator, we are not pretending to prove everything in 45 minutes.

teach.heading: Signs in ourselves
bullets: Our eyes, hearts and brains work together
Every person is different, with a different voice
Allah gave us the ability to think and speak
teach.note: Link to Qur’an 51:21 (‘and in yourselves, will you not see?’) as a pointer in your own words. Ask: which part of the body amazes you most? Let pupils share. Pause for a moment of silent reflection or a collective ‘Subhanallah’.

teach.heading: How do we respond?
bullets: Say Subhanallah and Alhamdulillah
Thank Allah for His blessings
Look after the earth: do not waste water or food
Be kind to animals and plants
teach.note: Explain that humans are trustees (khalifah) on the earth, so littering and wasting are not good character. Ask for one practical action at home. You may mention that the Prophet ﷺ was kind to animals, to keep the point warm, without quoting a specific wording.

practice: Write two signs of Allah from the sky and two from the earth.
Complete: When I see a beautiful sunset I can say ______.
Explain in a sentence why looking after the environment is part of being grateful.
independent: Draw a ‘Signs of Allah’ poster with six examples and a caption for each.
Write a paragraph beginning ‘I see the signs of Allah when ...’.
Make a pledge card with three actions that care for the earth.
exit: What is an ayah in the sense of a sign?
Give one way a Muslim can show thanks for creation.
lessons.homework: Go for a short walk or look out of a window and list five signs of Allah you notice, with a dhikr phrase for each.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use photographs for discussion and sentence starters; stretch: explain how reflecting on creation can strengthen iman.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: The Six Pillars of Iman
lessons.title: What is Iman? The hadith of Jibril
objectives: Explain what iman means
Name the six pillars of iman in order
Describe the setting of the hadith of Jibril

keywords.def: faith: believing in the heart and showing it by words and actions
a main foundation or support
the angel who brought revelation to the Prophets
Allah’s decree: everything happens by His knowledge and will

starter: Name one sign of Allah in creation.
What does ayah mean?
Why do Muslims say alhamdulillah?

teach.heading: A visitor in white
bullets: Umar ibn al-Khattab told this hadith, recorded by Muslim
A man in white clothes, with no sign of travel, came to the Prophet ﷺ
He asked about Islam, iman and ihsan
He was the angel Jibril, teaching the Companions their religion
teach.note: Tell it as a story. The Prophet ﷺ finished by telling Umar that this was Jibril who came to teach them their religion. Ask: why would the angel come to ask questions instead of just telling? (so that the Companions could hear the answers). This is reported by Imam Muslim; also in other collections.

teach.heading: The six pillars of iman
bullets: Belief in Allah
Belief in His angels
Belief in His books
Belief in His messengers
Belief in the Last Day
Belief in al-Qadr, the good and bad of it
teach.note: In the hadith the Prophet ﷺ said iman is to believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and to believe in the divine decree, its good and its bad. Teach a hand-and-heart gesture for each. Misconception: ‘five pillars’ vs ‘six pillars’. Five pillars are what we do; six pillars of iman are what we believe.

teach.heading: Iman and Islam
bullets: Islam: the five actions such as salah and fasting
Iman: what we believe in the heart
Ihsan: worship as if you see Allah
If you do not see Him, He sees you
teach.note: Present a simple table. For ihsan, read the meaning slowly: to worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, know that He sees you. Ask: how can ihsan make your prayer better? (Focus, slowing down.)

teach.heading: Strengthening our iman
bullets: Learn about Allah and His book
Make dhikr and du’a
Do good deeds and keep good company
Ask Allah to keep our hearts firm
teach.note: Iman increases with obedience and can weaken with sins; ahl as-sunnah hold this view. At Year 6 level, say it as ‘like a plant that needs water’. Ask pupils to pick one practical step.

practice: List the six pillars of iman in order.
True or false: Jibril came as a stranger to teach the Companions. Explain.
What is the difference between Islam and iman?
independent: Draw six pillars and label each with a one-line explanation.
Write four sentences retelling the hadith of Jibril in your own words.
Make a ‘ways to increase iman’ checklist with five ideas.
exit: Name the six pillars of iman.
lessons.homework: Teach the six pillars of iman to someone at home and write down their response.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pillars on picture cards to sequence; stretch: explain why belief and action go together.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: The Six Pillars of Iman
lessons.title: Belief in the angels and the holy books
objectives: Describe the angels and name four of them with their tasks
Name the revealed books
Explain why Muslims believe the Qur’an is preserved

keywords.def: honoured servants of Allah created from light who always obey Him
the book revealed to Prophet Musa (peace be upon him)
the book revealed to Prophet Isa (peace be upon him)
the final word of Allah revealed to Prophet Muhammad ﷺ

starter: List the six pillars of iman.
What is ihsan?
Who asked the Prophet ﷺ the questions in the hadith of Jibril?

teach.heading: Who are the angels?
bullets: Angels are created from light
They obey Allah and never disobey
We cannot normally see them
Belief in them is the second pillar
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. The hadith of Aisha in Sahih Muslim says angels were created from light, jinn from smokeless fire and Adam from what was described to you. Ask pupils: why believe in what we cannot see? (We trust Allah’s word, as we trust air exists though invisible.) Misconception: angels are not female or children of Allah and are not worshipped.

teach.heading: Four angels and their tasks
bullets: Jibril: brings revelation to the prophets
Mikail: in charge of rain and provision
Israfil: will blow the trumpet on the Last Day
The angel of death takes souls by Allah’s command
teach.note: Qur’an 32:11 speaks of ‘the angel of death who has been entrusted with you’; use that description rather than a personal name, since the Qur’an and authentic Sunnah do not name him. Also mention the recording angels (Qur’an 82:10-12). Ask: how does knowing angels record deeds change how we act?

teach.heading: The revealed books
bullets: Suhuf of Ibrahim (scrolls)
Tawrah to Musa and Zabur to Dawud
Injil to Isa
Qur’an to Muhammad ﷺ
teach.note: All the messengers brought the same core message: worship Allah alone. Muslims respect the earlier books as revealed, but the earlier texts were not preserved in their original form. The Qur’an is the final revelation and Allah promised to protect it (15:9: ‘Indeed it is We who sent down the Reminder and indeed We will guard it’).

teach.heading: The Qur’an is preserved
bullets: Memorised by the Companions and written down
Collected into one book under Abu Bakr and copied under Uthman
Millions of huffaz keep it in memory
Same Arabic text across the world
teach.note: Keep the facts simple and accurate: the revelation was written on materials and memorised; Abu Bakr gathered the pages into one collection after the battle of Yamamah on Umar’s advice; Uthman made copies from it. Ask: how do huffaz protect the Qur’an today?

teach.heading: Our response
bullets: Recite the Qur’an daily
Understand and follow its teachings
Respect the Qur’an: keep it clean and high
Love the angels and the messengers
teach.note: Invite one or two pupils to share what they are reciting at present. Stress that the response to belief is action: learn, read, apply.

practice: Match: Jibril / Mikail / Israfil to their task.
List the four books named in the lesson and the prophet each came to.
Why do Muslims believe the Qur’an is protected?
independent: Make a fact file on one angel using only what we know from the Qur’an and Sunnah.
Create a timeline of the revealed books.
Write a short paragraph: ‘What difference does belief in angels make to my day?’
exit: Name two holy books and their prophets.
lessons.homework: Recite your current surah to a family member and write one thing you learned from its meaning.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use a matching grid with images; stretch: explain similarities and differences between earlier books and the Qur’an.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Iman in depth: messengers, last day, qadar; fiqh of sawm
lessons.title: Belief in the messengers and their shared message
lessons.bigQuestion: If many different teachers all gave you the same main message, what would that tell you about the message?
objectives: To understand why Muslims believe in all of Allah's messengers and what message they all shared
successCriteria: All: name five messengers mentioned in the Qur'an
Most: explain the one message all messengers brought
Some: explain why Muhammad ﷺ is called the Seal of the Prophets
lessons.crossCurricular: History: placing events on a timeline in order, as with the order of the prophets from Adam to Muhammad ﷺ
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: respecting all the prophets of Allah

keywords.def: a messenger sent by Allah with a message
a prophet who receives revelation from Allah
the message and the mission of the messengers
believing Allah is One and worshipping Him alone
the last prophet: Muhammad ﷺ

hook.text: If many different teachers all gave you the same main message, what would that tell you about the message?
hook.a: That it comes from one source: every messenger brought the same message of tawheed from Allah.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'We did not send any messenger before you except that We revealed to him: there is no god except Me, so worship Me' (al-Anbiya 21:25). Belief in the messengers is the fourth pillar of iman.

starter.q: How many pillars of iman are there?
Which angel brought revelation to the prophets?
Which book was given to Musa?
What does tawheed mean?
starter.a: Believing Allah is One and worshipping Him alone

teach.heading: Who are the messengers?
bullets: People chosen by Allah to guide others
Sent to every nation (16:36)
25 are named in the Qur'an
Others Allah did not tell us about (4:164)
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Many scholars explain that every rasul is a nabi, but a rasul is sent with a message to deliver to people who have turned away. Allah says He sent a messenger to every nation saying 'worship Allah and avoid false gods' (an-Nahl 16:36), and that there are messengers whose stories He told and others He did not (an-Nisa 4:164). Ask: why would Allah send messengers to every people?

teach.heading: One shared message
teach.note: The centre is the message; around it are the prophets. Read 21:25. Every messenger called to tawheed, good character and the Hereafter, even though their laws could differ. Never show pictures of prophets.

teach.heading: What messengers are like
bullets: Human beings, not gods (18:110)
Truthful and trustworthy
They delivered the whole message
The best examples of character
teach.note: Al-Kahf 18:110: 'Say: I am only a man like you, to whom it has been revealed that your god is one God.' This guards against worshipping prophets. Muslims love and honour every prophet and say 'alayhis salam' after their names.

check.q: Which statement is TRUE about the messengers?
options: They all called people to worship Allah alone
Muslims believe only in Muhammad ﷺ
Each messenger brought a different god
check.why: 21:25 and 16:36: one message of tawheed. Muslims believe in all messengers (2:285); they were human (18:110).

teach.heading: The Seal of the Prophets
bullets: Muhammad ﷺ is the last prophet (33:40)
His message is for all people
We believe in all, without rejecting any (2:285)
teach.note: Al-Ahzab 33:40 calls him 'the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets'. A seal closes something: no prophet comes after him. Al-Baqarah 2:285: the believers say 'we make no distinction between any of His messengers' in belief. The five 'ulul 'azm' (messengers of great determination) are often listed as Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad ﷺ.

timeline.label: First
timeline.text: Adam, the first human and prophet

timeline.label: Then
timeline.text: Nuh calls his people for many years

timeline.label: Then
timeline.text: Ibrahim and Isma'il build the Ka'bah

timeline.label: Last
timeline.text: Muhammad ﷺ, Seal of the Prophets

practice.q: Put in order: Musa, Adam, Muhammad ﷺ, Ibrahim, Nuh.
practice.a: Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Muhammad ﷺ
practice.model: I do: start with the first human, Adam. Nuh came long after. Ibrahim came next and built the Ka'bah with Isma'il. Musa came from Ibrahim's descendants. Muhammad ﷺ is last, the Seal.

practice.q: What does 'Seal of the Prophets' mean?
practice.a: The last prophet: no prophet comes after Muhammad ﷺ

practice.q: Give the one message every messenger brought.
practice.a: Worship Allah alone (tawheed)

independent.q: In the portal response box, write a paragraph: 'Why do Muslims believe in all the messengers?' Use 21:25 and 2:285. Start: 'Muslims believe in all the messengers because ...'
independent.a: Because Allah sent them all with the same message of tawheed (21:25), and believers make no distinction between them (2:285); rejecting one is rejecting Allah's choice.
independent.model: Teacher models: 'Muslims believe in all the messengers because Allah sent every one of them. Allah says He revealed to each messenger that there is no god but Him (21:25) ...'

independent.q: Extend: name the five ulul 'azm.
independent.a: Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad ﷺ

independent.q: Stretch: why is it important that messengers were humans, not angels?
independent.a: So people could follow their example in real life; humans can copy a human (18:110).

exit.q: How many messengers are named in the Qur'an?
Who is the Seal of the Prophets?
exit.a: Muhammad ﷺ

exit.q: Back to our ponder: what does one shared message tell us?
exit.a: That all the messengers came from one God, Allah, with the same call to tawheed.

lessons.homework: Learn the names of ten prophets named in the Qur'an in order, and one fact about each.
lessons.send: SEND: name cards to order. EAL: sentence frame 'All the messengers taught ...'. Stretch: find 2:285 and copy the part about the messengers.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Seerah - the early life of the Prophet ﷺ
lessons.title: Arabia and the birth of the Prophet ﷺ
objectives: Describe what Makkah and Arabia were like before Islam
Retell the story of the Year of the Elephant
State when and where the Prophet ﷺ was born

keywords.def: the house of Allah in Makkah built by Ibrahim and Isma’il
the leading tribe of Makkah, the Prophet’s ﷺ tribe
the biography of the Prophet ﷺ
the period of ignorance before Islam

starter: Who is the last messenger of Allah?
What does ‘seerah’ mean?
Name two prophets who came before Muhammad ﷺ.

teach.heading: Arabia before Islam
bullets: Makkah was a trading town in a desert land
The Ka’bah was filled with idols
Tribes fought and the poor were treated badly
Some people still followed the religion of Ibrahim
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and salawat on the Prophet ﷺ. Show a map. Explain that Ibrahim and Isma’il had built the Ka’bah for the worship of Allah alone and that people had drifted into idol worship. Ask: what problems do we face when people forget Allah? Do not include invented details; keep to widely accepted facts.

teach.heading: The Year of the Elephant
bullets: Abrahah, a ruler from Yemen, marched on Makkah with an army and elephants
He wanted to destroy the Ka’bah
Allah sent flocks of birds with stones
Surah al-Fil (105) tells this story
teach.note: Recite or read Surah al-Fil (105) and explain: Abrahah’s army was destroyed. The Quraysh remembered it as the Year of the Elephant. Scholars record that the Prophet ﷺ was born around that year. Ask: what lesson does it teach about the House of Allah and about power?

teach.heading: The birth of the Prophet ﷺ
bullets: Born in Makkah, in the tribe of Quraysh, around 570 CE
His father Abdullah died before he was born
His mother was Aminah, his grandfather Abdul Muttalib
He was named Muhammad, ‘the praised one’
teach.note: Dates: the day of the week (Monday) is authentically reported in Muslim; the precise date is debated, so say ‘around 570 CE’. Do not claim a celebration date as a fact. Ask pupils to place Makkah on the map and draw a mini family tree.

teach.heading: A family tree
bullets: Descended from Prophet Ibrahim through Isma’il
Abdullah, Aminah, Abdul Muttalib, Abu Talib
Born into an honoured but not wealthy home
teach.note: Check understanding: who are the people in the tree and how are they related? Misconception: the Prophet ﷺ was not from a rich background; his uncle Abu Talib later took care of him.

practice: Place these events in order: Year of the Elephant, birth of the Prophet ﷺ, building of the Ka’bah.
What was Abrahah trying to do and what happened?
Name the Prophet’s ﷺ mother and grandfather.
independent: Write a short newspaper report about the Year of the Elephant.
Draw a simple map of Arabia with Makkah marked and two facts about it.
Create a family tree for the Prophet ﷺ with the names learned.
exit: In which tribe was the Prophet ﷺ born?
Which surah tells the story of the elephant?
lessons.homework: Learn Surah al-Fil with its meaning and write three sentences about the lesson.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sequencing cards with captions and pictures of places; stretch: compare the state of Makkah before and after Islam.

the Prophet’s ﷺ first wife and the first to believe
a trust that must be returned or protected

People left their valuables with him
He worked as a shepherd and a trader
Honesty was his habit even before prophethood

Muhammad ﷺ placed it on a cloak so every tribe could lift it

She asked him to trade for her; he was honest and successful
They married when he was about twenty-five
She supported him in all that followed

lessons.title: Salah: the daily meeting with Allah
objectives: Name the five daily prayers and their rak’ahs
Explain why salah is important
Describe the main actions in one rak’ah

keywords.def: the ritual prayer, the second pillar of Islam
one unit of prayer
the direction of the Ka’bah
prostration with the forehead on the ground

starter: Name the first step of wudu.
What do we say after finishing wudu?
Which pillar of Islam is salah?

teach.heading: Why do we pray?
bullets: “Establish prayer for My remembrance” (20:14)
Salah connects us to Allah five times a day
It teaches discipline, humility and gratitude
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Ask: who do you talk to when you are worried or happy? Salah is our appointment with Allah. Say that the five daily prayers were made obligatory on the night of the Mi’raj (we will study this in Year 8).

teach.heading: The five prayers
bullets: Fajr: 2 rak’ahs before sunrise
Dhuhr: 4 rak’ahs after midday
Asr: 4 rak’ahs in the afternoon
Maghrib: 3 rak’ahs after sunset
Isha: 4 rak’ahs at night
teach.note: Show a prayer timetable for the local area. Check in on the obligatory rak’ahs only. Pupils make a mnemonic. Ask: which prayer do you find hardest to keep? Encourage honesty and support.

teach.heading: Inside a rak’ah
bullets: Stand facing the qiblah, say Allahu akbar
Recite al-Fatihah and a short surah
Bow (ruku’), stand, then prostrate (sujud)
Sit between two sujuds and repeat
teach.note: Demonstrate carefully. At the end of the second rak’ah (and last) we sit for tashahhud then give salam to right and left. Remind pupils that adults will correct details; we are learning the outline. Mention the beauty of sujud: ‘the closest a servant is to his Lord is while in prostration’ (Sahih Muslim, Abu Hurayrah) - paraphrase is fine.

teach.heading: Praying with khushu’
bullets: Put away distractions and slow down
Understand what you recite
Pray on time
Ask Allah in sujud
teach.note: Ask pupils to share one tip for staying focused. Link to ihsan from lesson 4: worship as if you see Him.

practice: Complete the table of five prayers and rak’ahs.
Put the actions of a rak’ah in order.
Give two benefits of praying on time.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Iman in depth: messengers, last day, qadar; fiqh of sawm
lessons.title: Fiqh of sawm before Ramadan: intention, what breaks the fast and who is excused
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do you think Allah made fasting about more than just being hungry?
objectives: To understand the main rules of fasting so that I can fast correctly and help others to
successCriteria: All: say when the fast starts and ends and why niyyah matters
Most: sort actions into ones that break the fast and ones that do not
Some: explain who is excused from fasting and what they do instead
lessons.crossCurricular: Science (Year 6 circulation and health): why drinking water at suhur and iftar keeps the body healthy
lessons.smsc: Moral: keeping a promise to Allah even when no one else can see

keywords.def: fasting: no food or drink from dawn to sunset, for Allah
intention: deciding in the heart why you do something
the meal eaten before dawn
breaking the fast at sunset
making up a missed fast on another day
feeding a poor person for each day when someone can never fast

hook.text: Why do you think Allah made fasting about more than just being hungry?
hook.a: Fasting builds taqwa (2:183): self-control, gratitude and remembering Allah all day, not only an empty stomach.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'O you who believe, fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, so that you may gain taqwa' (al-Baqarah 2:183). Fasting in Ramadan is one of the five pillars of Islam, and we learn its rules so that our fast is correct.

starter.q: Fasting in Ramadan is one of ...
What does taqwa mean?
starter.a: Being aware of Allah and careful to obey Him
options: Being aware of Allah and careful to obey Him

starter.q: In which month was the Qur'an first revealed?
Name one thing you remember about fasting from Year 5.
starter.a: For example: from dawn to sunset; we fast to gain taqwa; the sick are excused

teach.heading: What is sawm?
bullets: No food or drink from dawn to sunset
Fajr starts the fast; maghrib ends it
Made with niyyah, for Allah alone
Fard in Ramadan on adults who are able
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Allah describes the white thread of dawn becoming clear from the black thread, then completing the fast until night (al-Baqarah 2:187). The intention is in the heart: deciding to fast for Allah. Many scholars say the intention for a Ramadan fast is made before fajr. Children who are not yet adults are not required to fast but are encouraged to practise.

teach.heading: Breaks the fast or not?
teach.note: Go through each card. Key teaching: eating or drinking ON PURPOSE breaks the fast. The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever forgets while fasting and eats or drinks should complete the fast, because Allah fed him and gave him drink (Bukhari and Muslim). Swallowing your own saliva, showering and cleaning teeth with a miswak do not break it.

cards: A. Eating a snack on purpose
B. Eating because you forgot you were fasting
F. Cleaning teeth with a miswak
H. Drinking water at lunch knowing you are fasting

teach.heading: Who is excused?
bullets: The ill and travellers: make up the days later (2:184)
Elderly people who cannot fast: fidyah, feeding the poor
Pregnant or nursing mothers, as scholars explain
Children: not required, but practise
teach.note: Al-Baqarah 2:184 says whoever is ill or on a journey fasts the same number of other days, and those who can only fast with great hardship give fidyah, feeding a poor person. Make the point that Islam is a religion of ease: 'Allah intends ease for you, not hardship' (2:185). Qada' means making up a missed day.

check.q: Yusuf has a high fever on the 3rd of Ramadan. What should he do?
options: Not fast while ill and make up the day later
Fast anyway, even if it harms him
Pay fidyah and never make it up
check.why: The ill are excused and make up the days (2:184). Fasting is not meant to harm. Fidyah is for those who can never fast, such as the very elderly.

teach.heading: Sunnah of fasting
bullets: Eat suhur: there is blessing in it
Break the fast quickly at sunset
Break it with dates or water
Guard the tongue: no lies or bad words
teach.note: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Take suhur, for in suhur there is blessing' (Bukhari and Muslim). He said people will remain upon good as long as they hasten to break the fast (Bukhari and Muslim). Breaking the fast with dates, or water if there are none, is reported in Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi. He also said whoever does not give up false speech, Allah has no need of him giving up food and drink (Bukhari).

practice.q: Maryam drinks water at 2 pm, then remembers she is fasting. Is her fast broken? What should she do?
practice.a: No, it is not broken because she forgot. She stops drinking as soon as she remembers and carries on fasting.
practice.model: I do: 1) Did she do it on purpose? No, she forgot. 2) What did the Prophet ﷺ teach? Whoever forgets and eats or drinks completes the fast (Bukhari and Muslim). 3) So her fast is fine; she stops when she remembers.

practice.q: Ali eats crisps at 4 pm because he feels like it, knowing he is fasting. Broken or not?
practice.a: Broken: he ate on purpose. He must make up the day (qada') and repent.

practice.q: When exactly does the fast end each day?
practice.a: At sunset, the time of maghrib

independent.q: Write a 'How to fast' guide for a younger child in the portal response box: when to start, when to stop, what breaks the fast, who is excused, two Sunnahs. Start: 'Fasting means ...'
independent.a: Covers dawn to sunset, niyyah, eating or drinking on purpose breaks it, forgetting does not, the ill and travellers make up days, suhur and quick iftar.
independent.model: Teacher writes the first two lines: 'Fasting means not eating or drinking from dawn to sunset, for Allah. First, make your niyyah in your heart before fajr ...'

independent.q: Extend: what is the difference between qada' and fidyah?
independent.a: Qada' is making up a missed fast later; fidyah is feeding a poor person for each day when someone can never fast.

independent.q: Stretch: why do you think Allah excuses the ill and travellers?
independent.a: Because Islam is ease, not hardship (2:185); Allah does not want fasting to harm us.

exit.q: Which of these breaks the fast?
exit.a: Drinking water on purpose

exit.q: A traveller misses three fasts. What does he do?
exit.a: Makes up three days later (qada')

exit.q: Back to our ponder: why is fasting more than being hungry?
exit.a: It builds taqwa: obeying Allah when no one sees, self-control and gratitude.

lessons.title: Belief in the Last Day and accountability
lessons.bigQuestion: If you knew every single action you do was being written down, would you change anything today?
objectives: To understand what Muslims believe about the Last Day and how it shapes the way they live now
successCriteria: All: put the main stages after death in order
Most: explain what accountability means for a Muslim
Some: explain how belief in the Last Day changes everyday choices
lessons.smsc: Moral: taking responsibility for our own actions

keywords.def: the life after this world, which lasts for ever
the Last Day, the Day of Judgement
the stage in the grave between death and the Last Day
having to answer for what you did
the scales that weigh deeds on the Last Day

hook.text: If you knew every single action you do was being written down, would you change anything today?
hook.a: Muslims believe the angels record every deed and every person will see their record on the Last Day.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it' (az-Zalzalah 99:7-8). Belief in the Last Day is the fifth pillar of iman.

starter.q: Name the fourth pillar of iman.
Who is the Seal of the Prophets?
What did every messenger call people to?
Which ayah says no messenger was sent without the message 'worship Me'?

teach.heading: This life is not the end
bullets: Every soul will taste death
The barzakh: the life of the grave
Then the Day of Resurrection
Then Jannah or Jahannam, for ever
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Keep the tone calm and hopeful. 'Every soul will taste death' (Al Imran 3:185). Behind those who die is a barrier (barzakh) until the Day they are resurrected (al-Mu'minun 23:100). Only Allah knows when the Last Day will be.

timeline.text: Death: the soul leaves the body
Barzakh: the life of the grave

teach.heading: Our record of deeds
bullets: Angels write every deed (82:10-12)
Nothing is left out
Records given in the right or left hand
Good deeds weigh heavy on the scales
teach.note: Al-Infitar 82:10-12: noble angels record and know what you do. Al-Haqqah 69:19: the one given his book in his right hand will say 'read my record'. Al-Anbiya 21:47: Allah sets up just scales, and no soul is wronged at all.

check.q: What does 'accountability' mean for a Muslim?
options: Answering to Allah for what we do
Only being judged by other people
Deeds do not matter if no one sees
check.why: We answer to Allah, who sees everything; even an atom's weight counts (99:7-8). Hidden or small deeds still count.

teach.heading: Allah is Just and Merciful
bullets: No one is wronged, not even a little
Allah's mercy is greater than His anger
Tawbah wipes away sins
Good deeds can erase bad deeds
teach.note: Balance hope and fear. 21:47: no soul is wronged. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim says Allah wrote that His mercy prevails over His anger. Hud 11:114: good deeds remove bad deeds. Pupils should leave feeling hopeful and motivated, not frightened.

teach.heading: How it changes today
teach.note: Ask pupils to add one more row of their own in the chat.

left.title: Without thinking of the Last Day

practice.q: Put in order: judgement, death, resurrection, barzakh, Jannah or Jahannam.
practice.a: Death, barzakh, resurrection, judgement, Jannah or Jahannam
practice.model: I do: first death, when the soul leaves the body. Next the barzakh, the grave. Then everyone is raised (resurrection). Then the records and scales (judgement). Last, the final home.

practice.q: What do the angels in 82:10-12 do?
practice.a: They record our deeds

practice.q: Give one way remembering the Last Day helps you at school.
practice.a: For example: doing my own work honestly even in a test no one checks.

independent.q: In the portal response box, write a diary entry for one day, showing three choices you made because you believe in the Last Day. Start: 'Today I remembered that ...'
independent.a: Three realistic choices (honesty, kindness, prayer on time) each linked to accountability or the record of deeds.
independent.model: Teacher writes: 'Today I remembered that every deed is written. When I found a pound coin in the corridor I handed it in, because ...'

independent.q: Extend: explain 99:7-8 in your own words.
independent.a: Even the smallest good or bad deed will be seen and counted on the Last Day.

independent.q: Stretch: why does Islam teach both hope and fear about the Last Day?
independent.a: Fear stops us doing wrong; hope in Allah's mercy keeps us trying and making tawbah.

exit.q: What is the barzakh?
exit.a: The life of the grave between death and the Last Day

exit.q: Even an atom's weight of good will be ...
exit.a: Seen (99:7)

exit.q: Back to our ponder: would you change anything today? What, and why?
exit.a: For example: being more honest or kinder, because every deed is recorded.

lessons.title: Belief in qadar: trust in Allah and effort
lessons.bigQuestion: If Allah already knows everything that will happen, why should you still work hard for a test?
objectives: To understand what belief in qadar means and why Muslims put in effort while trusting Allah
successCriteria: All: say what qadar means and give the ayah 54:49
Most: name the four parts of belief in qadar
Some: explain how tawakkul and effort work together, with an example
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE (Spring 1 Money matters, achieving goals): planning and working towards a goal
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: patience and trust in Allah when things go wrong

keywords.def: Allah's decree: Allah knows, writes, wills and creates all things
trusting Allah after doing your best
trying hard and doing your part
patience, especially in hard times
the choice Allah gives us, for which we are responsible

hook.text: If Allah already knows everything that will happen, why should you still work hard for a test?
hook.a: Allah's knowledge does not force our choices; we are told to work hard and trust Him (tie your camel and trust).

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Indeed, We have created all things with qadar (a measure and decree)' (al-Qamar 54:49). Belief in qadar, the good and the bad of it, is the sixth pillar of iman, as taught in the hadith of Jibril (Muslim).

starter.q: What is the barzakh?
What will happen to an atom's weight of good?
Name the six pillars of iman.
starter.a: Allah, angels, books, messengers, the Last Day, qadar

teach.heading: What is qadar?
bullets: Allah's decree over all things (54:49)
Nothing happens outside Allah's knowledge
The sixth pillar of iman
We believe in its good and its bad
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. In the hadith of Jibril (Muslim), the Prophet ﷺ listed the pillars of iman ending with qadar, its good and its bad. Explain: what seems bad to us can contain good we do not see (al-Baqarah 2:216: you may dislike a thing while it is good for you).

teach.heading: Four parts of qadar
teach.note: Scholars of ahl as-sunnah explain belief in qadar in four parts: Allah KNOWS everything; He WROTE it in the Preserved Tablet; nothing happens unless He WILLS it; He CREATES all things. Give a simple example for each.

items: Will: nothing happens unless Allah wills

teach.heading: Trust AND effort
bullets: A man asked: tie my camel or trust Allah?
The Prophet ﷺ said: tie it and trust
We plan, work hard, then rely on Allah (65:3)
We are responsible for our choices
teach.note: The camel hadith is reported by at-Tirmidhi. At-Talaq 65:3: whoever relies on Allah, He is sufficient for him. The Prophet ﷺ also said: 'Strive for what benefits you, seek help from Allah, and do not give up' (Muslim). Qadar is never an excuse for laziness or wrongdoing.

check.q: Sara says: 'It's all written, so I won't revise.' What is wrong?
options: We must make effort AND trust Allah
Qadar means Allah does not know
check.why: The camel hadith: tie it and trust. We choose and are responsible; effort is part of what Allah has decreed for success.

teach.heading: When things go wrong
bullets: Do not say 'if only I had ...'
Say: Allah decreed, and what He willed He did
Be patient: sabr brings reward
Learn, then try again
teach.note: In the same hadith in Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ taught that if something befalls you, do not say 'if only I had done ...' but say 'qaddara Allahu wa ma sha'a fa'al' (قَدَّرَ اللَّهُ وَمَا شَاءَ فَعَلَ): Allah decreed, and what He willed He did. 'If only' opens the door to the work of Shaytan. Contrast with learning from a mistake, which is good.

practice.q: Hamza's team lost the quiz final after weeks of practice. What would a person who believes in qadar say and do?
practice.a: Say 'qaddara Allahu wa ma sha'a fa'al', be patient, thank Allah for the effort, learn what to improve and try again.
practice.model: I do: 1) What happened is from Allah's decree, so no 'if only'. 2) He did his part: practice was the effort. 3) Respond with sabr and say 'qaddara Allahu wa ma sha'a fa'al'. 4) Learn and try again next time.

practice.q: True or false: believing in qadar means we do not need to try.
practice.a: False: we tie the camel and trust

practice.q: Which ayah says Allah created all things with qadar?
practice.a: Al-Qamar 54:49

independent.q: In the portal response box, write advice to a friend who failed a spelling test and says 'it was written, there's no point'. Use the camel hadith. Start: 'Dear friend, I understand ...'
independent.a: Kind tone; explains qadar does not cancel effort; tie your camel; makes a plan to revise; trusts Allah; avoids 'if only'.
independent.model: Teacher writes: 'Dear friend, I understand you feel upset. The Prophet ﷺ told a man to tie his camel and then trust Allah. That means ...'

independent.q: Extend: name the four parts of belief in qadar.
independent.a: Knowledge, writing, will, creation

independent.q: Stretch: how does believing in qadar help someone stay calm in a hard time?
independent.a: They know nothing happens outside Allah's knowledge and wisdom, so they are patient and hopeful (2:216).

exit.q: Tawakkul means ...
exit.a: Trusting Allah after doing your best
options: Trusting Allah after doing your best

exit.q: What should a Muslim say instead of 'if only'?
exit.a: Qaddara Allahu wa ma sha'a fa'al
options: Qaddara Allahu wa ma sha'a fa'al

exit.q: Back to our ponder: why still work hard if Allah knows everything?
exit.a: Because Allah commands effort and we are responsible for our choices; tie the camel and trust.

lessons.homework: Set one goal for the week, write the effort you will make each day and a du'a asking Allah for success.
lessons.send: SEND: four symbol cards for the four parts. EAL: camel story told with a picture of a tied camel. Stretch: compare 2:216 and 54:49.

lessons.title: How iman shows in character; unit quiz and preparing for Ramadan
lessons.bigQuestion: How could someone tell you have iman without you saying a word?
objectives: To understand how true belief shows itself in good character and actions
successCriteria: All: give three actions the Prophet ﷺ linked to iman
Most: answer the unit quiz on messengers, the Last Day, qadar and sawm
Some: plan how to build one quality of character in Ramadan

keywords.def: belief in the heart, said with the tongue, shown in actions
character and manners
modesty and shyness from doing wrong
voluntary charity, money or good deeds
sincerity: doing things for Allah alone

hook.text: How could someone tell you have iman without you saying a word?
hook.a: Through character: honesty, kindness, modesty, helping others and good speech.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say what is good or stay silent; let him honour his neighbour; let him honour his guest' (Bukhari and Muslim). Iman is meant to be seen in how we treat people.

starter.q: What does tawakkul mean?
starter.a: Trusting Allah after doing your best
options: Trusting Allah after doing your best

starter.q: What is qada'?
What is the barzakh?
Who brought revelation to the messengers?

teach.heading: Iman has branches
bullets: Iman has over seventy branches
Highest: la ilaha illa Allah
Lowest: moving harm from the road
Haya' is a branch of iman
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. This hadith is reported by Muslim (Bukhari reports 'over sixty'). It shows iman is belief AND action. Ask: what 'harm on the road' could you move today? (A banana skin, a bike in a doorway.)

teach.heading: Belief that shows
bullets: Say good or stay silent
Honour your neighbour and guest
Love for others what you love for yourself
The best in iman are best in character
teach.note: Speak good or stay silent; neighbour; guest (Bukhari and Muslim). 'None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself' (Bukhari and Muslim). The most complete believers in iman are those with the best character (Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi).

check.q: Which action shows the link between iman and character best?
options: Speaking kindly to a new pupil
check.why: Good speech and kindness are signs of iman in the hadith. Showing off and selfishness are not.

teach.heading: Unit quiz
bullets: Ten questions on the unit
Messengers, Last Day, qadar, sawm
Answer in the Teams Form
Mark it together
teach.note: Run the unit quiz as the independent task (Teams Forms quiz, 10 questions, 8 minutes). Questions are in the independent section; go through answers together and note gaps for Spring 2 starters.

teach.heading: Getting ready for Ramadan
bullets: Renew a sincere intention: for Allah
Choose one character goal
Plan extra Qur'an and du'a
Plan one act of sadaqah
teach.note: Ramadan begins around the end of this half term (the date depends on the moon sighting). Link sawm (lesson 1) with character: the fast is not only from food but also from bad speech. Smiling at your brother is sadaqah (at-Tirmidhi).

practice.q: Turn this into a 'character action': 'Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his neighbour.'
practice.a: For example: take a plate of food to our neighbour, or help carry their shopping.
practice.model: I do: 1) Find the instruction: honour your neighbour. 2) Think who my neighbour is. 3) Choose a real action: take them some food at iftar. 4) Do it for Allah (ikhlas).

practice.q: Moving a stone from the road is ...
practice.a: A branch of iman

independent.q: Unit quiz (Teams Forms, 10 questions): 1) Fasting begins at? 2) Does eating by mistake break the fast? 3) Who makes up missed fasts? 4) Messengers named in the Qur'an? 5) Seal of the Prophets? 6) Message of all messengers? 7) Barzakh? 8) 99:7-8 teaches? 9) Four parts of qadar? 10) Camel hadith teaches?
independent.a: 1) Dawn (fajr) 2) No 3) The ill and travellers (qada') 4) 25 5) Muhammad ﷺ 6) Worship Allah alone 7) The life of the grave 8) Every good and bad deed will be seen 9) Knowledge, writing, will, creation 10) Make effort and trust Allah
independent.model: Teacher answers question 1 aloud first: 'Fasting begins at dawn, the time of fajr, as 2:187 describes the white thread of dawn.'

independent.q: Extend: write your Ramadan character goal and three steps to reach it in the portal response box.
independent.a: For example: speak only good; step 1 count my unkind words, step 2 say 'I'm fasting' when angry, step 3 make du'a.

independent.q: Stretch: explain how sawm and good character are linked.
independent.a: Fasting trains self-control; the Prophet ﷺ said Allah has no need of the fast of someone who does not leave false speech (Bukhari).

exit.q: Which of these is a branch of iman?
exit.a: Haya' (modesty)

exit.q: Back to our ponder: how could someone tell you have iman?
exit.a: From my character: honesty, kindness, good speech, helping others.

lessons.homework: Do your Ramadan character goal for three days and write what you did in a short journal.
lessons.send: SEND: quiz read aloud with two options per question. EAL: quiz key words pre-taught. Stretch: write a short reflection on the hadith of love for your brother.

keywords.def: successor: the leader of the Muslims after the Prophet ﷺ
the four Rightly Guided Caliphs
the truthful: Abu Bakr's title
consultation: deciding by discussion

hook.text: When a great leader dies, what does a community need most in the next few days?
hook.a: Calm, truth and a trustworthy new leader: Abu Bakr gave all three.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Muhammad is not but a messenger; other messengers have passed on before him' (Al 'Imran 3:144). Abu Bakr recited it to steady the believers.

starter.q: Bismillah. Belief in qadar means ...
starter.a: Believing everything happens by Allah's decree
options: Believing everything happens by Allah's decree

starter.q: How many pillars of iman are there?
In which year did the Hijrah happen?

teach.heading: The four Rightly Guided Caliphs
teach.note: Show the order and dates.

teach.heading: A day of sadness
bullets: The Prophet ﷺ died in 632 CE
Some could not believe it
Abu Bakr calmed everyone with the truth
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Abu Bakr said: whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad has died; whoever worships Allah, Allah is alive and does not die; then he recited Al 'Imran 3:144 (Bukhari).

teach.heading: Choosing the leader
bullets: The Companions met and discussed (shura)
They chose Abu Bakr
He was the Prophet's ﷺ closest friend
teach.note: The meeting at the Saqifah of Banu Sa'idah is reported in Bukhari. Abu Bakr had led the prayers during the Prophet's ﷺ last illness (Bukhari and Muslim).

teach.heading: Quick check
bullets: Think, then vote
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.why: The order is Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali.

practice.q: Explain why the Companions chose Abu Bakr.
practice.a: He was the Prophet's ﷺ closest companion, truthful, had led the prayers in the Prophet's ﷺ illness, and was chosen by consultation.
practice.model: Point: Abu Bakr was the most trusted Companion. Evidence: he led the prayers in the Prophet's ﷺ last illness (Bukhari and Muslim). Explain: the Companions consulted and agreed on him. Link: leadership in Islam is a trust.

practice.q: Put in order: Uthman, Abu Bakr, Ali, Umar.
practice.a: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali

practice.q: Khalifah means ...
practice.a: Successor

independent.q: Make a caliph fact file for Abu Bakr on the pupil PDF (title, dates, how chosen, one quality), then write in the portal response box why his speech mattered. Start: 'Abu Bakr's words mattered because ...'
independent.a: Accurate fact file; speech kept Muslims focused on worshipping Allah alone
independent.model: Teacher fills 'Title: as-Siddiq, the truthful' and 'Dates: 632 to 634 CE'.

independent.q: Extend: what does 3:144 teach?
independent.a: Muhammad ﷺ is a messenger; messengers before him died; Islam continues.

independent.q: Stretch: why is shura a good way to choose a leader?
independent.a: People discuss, share wisdom and agree together.

exit.q: The first caliph was ...
exit.a: Abu Bakr

exit.q: Back to our ponder: what did the community need, and how did Abu Bakr help?
exit.a: Calm, truth and a trusted leader: he reminded them Allah is alive.

hook.text: If something very precious is kept only in people's memories, how could you make sure it is never lost?
hook.a: Write it down carefully, checked against memory: as Abu Bakr had the Qur'an gathered.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian' (al-Hijr 15:9).

starter.q: Bismillah. The first caliph was ...
Shura means ...
Abu Bakr's title as-Siddiq means ...

teach.heading: A firm leader
bullets: He sent Usamah's army as the Prophet ﷺ had planned
He stood firm when some refused zakah
He kept the ummah united
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Keep the wars of that time brief and factual.

teach.heading: Why gather the Qur'an?
bullets: At Yamamah, many huffaz were killed
Umar feared parts could be lost
Abu Bakr agreed after thinking carefully
teach.note: Reported in Bukhari.

teach.heading: How it was done

check.q: Who gathered the Qur'an for Abu Bakr?

practice.q: Explain why the Qur'an was gathered into one copy.

practice.model: Point: to protect the Qur'an. Evidence: many huffaz died at Yamamah, and Umar advised Abu Bakr (Bukhari). Explain: written pieces were checked against memory and gathered. Link: Allah promised to protect the Qur'an (15:9).

practice.q: Where were many huffaz killed?

practice.q: Who suggested gathering the Qur'an?

independent.a: Correct steps; Zayd was young, trusted, a scribe of revelation and careful
independent.model: Teacher draws box 1: 'Yamamah: many huffaz killed' with an arrow to box 2.

independent.q: Extend: who kept the copy after Abu Bakr?
independent.a: Umar, then Hafsah

independent.q: Stretch: link this to 15:9.
independent.a: Allah promised to protect the Qur'an; the gathering is one way He did it.

exit.q: A mushaf is ...
exit.a: A written copy of the Qur'an
options: A written copy of the Qur'an

exit.q: Back to our ponder: how do you protect something precious kept in memory?
exit.a: Write it carefully and check it against memory.
